title: Tokenization Visualizer
creator: Dan McCreary
subject: Artificial Intelligence
Large Language Models
Tokenization
Tokens
description: Type a sentence and compare how a person splits it into words with how a language model splits it into tokens. An illustrative rule-based tokenizer (not a real model's tokenizer) breaks long or unusual words into several colored token chips, and a word count and token count are shown side by side.

learningObjectives: Explain why a language model's cost and capacity are measured in tokens rather than words.
Compare the word count of a sentence with its token count.
Predict that long or unusual words split into more tokens than short common words.
prerequisites: Knows that a large language model predicts the next unit of text

controls.label: Your text
controls.description: Sentence to tokenize, up to 120 characters; Enter runs Tokenize

controls.label: Tokenize
controls.description: Re-runs the split on the current text with one quick transition from word boxes to token chips

controls.label: Token chip
controls.description: Opens an infobox with the token's text, position index, and why it split there

assumptions: The splitter is a hand-written approximation, not the tokenizer of any real model
Short or common words stay whole; familiar beginnings and endings split off; long unfamiliar stretches break into fragments of four letters
limitations: Token counts will not match any real model's token counts
Spaces are not shown as part of tokens

pedagogical.teachingStrategy: Predict, then reveal: the learner types a sentence, predicts the token count, and checks it
keyQuestions: Why is the token count usually larger than the word count?
Which kinds of words split into the most tokens?
commonMisconceptions: One word always equals one token
A model's limits and prices are measured in words or characters
assessmentOpportunities: Explain to a colleague why a 1,000-word document does not cost 1,000 units to send to a model
